name: Aruan
confidence_why: The only description of Aruan, Ferreira Penna's 1881 wordlist taken from the last speaker, marks a 'dominant' syllable on each word (mostly penultimate, some final) but states no rule and uses its accents partly for vowel length, and Nimuendajú 1948, Loukotka 1968 and Ribeiro 2010 say nothing about stress, so no placement or type can be defended.
catalog_citation: Ferreira Penna, Domingos Soares. 1881. Algumas palavras da lingua dos indios Aruans. Archivos do Museu Nacional do Rio de Janeiro 4: 15-25 (text dated Belém, 8 May 1879; Glottolog dates it 1879). Google Books scan re-hosted by Biblioteca Digital Curt Nimuendajú.
catalog_locator: p. 19, section 'Accentos e syllabas'; wordlist p. 21 (image) for the accent-marked forms.
catalog_quote: Para representar com clareza as flexões das palavras, eu emprego, não só os dous accentos mais usados, mas tambem o grave ou inclinado. O accento agudo é sempre sobre-posto à syllaba dominante, sendo as outras breves ou semi-longas; semi-longas serão as que tiverem accento grave ou circumflexo. Quando a palavra não tiver accento agudo, a syllaba dominante será aquella em que se achar o u allemão ou um diphtongo. As syllabas terminaes, em cuja vogal não ha accento, são sempre breves.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.quote: O accento agudo é sempre sobre-posto à syllaba dominante, sendo as outras breves ou semi-longas; semi-longas serão as que tiverem accento grave ou circumflexo. Quando a palavra não tiver accento agudo, a syllaba dominante será aquella em que se achar o u allemão ou um diphtongo. As syllabas terminaes, em cuja vogal não ha accento, são sempre breves.
new_statements.translation: The acute accent is always placed over the dominant syllable, the others being short or semi-long; semi-long are those bearing a grave or circumflex accent. When a word has no acute accent, the dominant syllable is the one containing the German u or a diphthong. Final syllables whose vowel bears no accent are always short.
new_statements.citation: Ferreira Penna, Domingos Soares. 1881. Algumas palavras da lingua dos indios Aruans. Archivos do Museu Nacional do Rio de Janeiro 4: 15-25.
new_statements.locator: p. 19, section 'Accentos e syllabas' (PDF page 8; page scan the page scan verified against the scanned)
new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (14 pp., Google Books scan re-hosted by Biblioteca Digital Curt Nimuendaju, no text) and viewed the page scan = journal p. 19 (header 'ARCHIVOS DO MUSEU NACIONAL 19'). Under the heading 'Accentos e syllabas' the three sentences of the quote are on the page exactly as given: 'O accento agudo é sempre sobre-posto à syllaba dominante, sendo as outras breves ou semi-longas; semi-longas serão as que tiverem accento grave ou circumflexo. Quando a palavra não tiver accento agudo, a syllaba dominante será aquella em que se achar o u allemão ou um diphtongo. As syllabas terminaes, em cuja vogal não ha accento, são sempre breves.' (scanned file lines 266-271 has the same text with scanned nois…
new_statements.rule_in_words: The only first-hand source states no positional rule: the collector marks the stressed ('dominant') syllable of each word with an acute accent, treats grave/circumflex vowels as semi-long, and says that words without an acute are stressed on the syllable containing [ü] or a diphthong, with unaccented final syllables always short. Stress is therefore recorded item by item, not generalised. My own tally of the acute marks on two list pages (journal pp. 20 and 22, images p-10/p-11) gives roughly 18 clearly penultimate forms (eytána, yçahále, púdy, lápu, kuáke, mamíke, ucatáca, amáde, adamána, naráya, uarábo..) against about 6 final (p'partán, caláy, tepáuctekúy, analáu, kumatú, álamáy), i.e. predominantly penultimate in citation forms, but this is a reader's count, not the source's claim.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; a few forms carry two acutes (álamáy, tepáuctekúy), which Penna does not explain.
new_statements.exceptions: Words without an acute mark: stress falls on the syllable with 'u allemão' ([ü]) or a diphthong. The vowel of the body-part prefix pe- is 'essentially mute' (p. 19, 'Prefixa').
new_statements.domain_note: Citation forms in a 224-item wordlist elicited in 1877 at Afuá (Marajó) from the last speaker, Anselmo José (~75 years old), who had not used the language for years; Penna himself warns of 'variation or incoherence' in his data. Orthographic-convention statement, not a phonological analysis.
new_statements.identity_note: Penna's 1877/1881 list is the Marajó (Afuá) variety from the last local speaker; Nimuendajú's 1926 30-word list is from Aruã descendants on the Uaçá River, Amapá. Both are the same Glottolog language arua1264 (Aruan). Loukotka 1968 groups a second, otherwise unattested language 'Sacaca' (eastern Marajó, B. San Antonio ms.) with Aruan; nothing on it was found. The earlier scan note called it 'Aruan of Marajó known from old wordlists', which matches.

sources.note: pp. 18-19 'Notas sobre a pronunciação' and 'Accentos e syllabas': the acute accent is always written over the 'syllaba dominante' (stressed syllable), other syllables being short or semi-long (grave/circumflex = semi-long); when a word has no acute, the dominant syllable is the one with German u or a diphthong; unaccented final syllables are always short. No positional rule is stated; stress is marked word by word in the 224-item list.
